topInterview.title: INTERVIEW
topInterview.contentTitle: This fall, Joon Whang is doing a tutorial with the theater department called “Politics in Dramatic Literature”
topInterview.content:
What’s your tutorial about?
While Joon was initially inspired to do a directing tutorial following his involvement in one-acts last spring, the nature of his studies have since evolved into dramaturgy. Joon and Laurie began by analyzing the fall play, Twelve Angry Men, examining it in the political context in which it was written, as well as the context of the playwright’s own philosphy. Additionally, Joon and Laurie have discussed the play’s relevance in a modern political context. All of these factors, Joon noted, are important for directors to consider and the final production of Twelve Angry Men will likely include some of their findings.
Joon found these discussions got him interested in the idea of political theater as a whole, so they then decided to look beyond the fall play at The Crucible.
What got you interested in this idea?
Directing and acting in the one-act festival last spring sparked Joon’s interest, as he says he appreciates how as a director one must look at all the combined elements of theater, including coaching acting, staging. With regard to staging in particular, Joon noted, “Say you have two people reading a scene and one is standing up and one is sitting down, what’s the message there?” Joon wanted to explore these subtleties.
What ties between politics and theater do you see historically? In current events? In reading The Crucible, Joon says he’s looking through its original historic lens of “Mccarthyism, lack of freedom of speech, regulations, the idea of a witch hunt.” He also noted how the play’s suggestions of Racial prejudice parallel the modern era’s criminal justice system, which is also related to the fall play.
What are some of your greatest takeaways right now?
“The amount of layers you have to look through,” Joon said. These layers include how casting influences the play, the impact of modern problems on an audience’s reception of its content, consideration of the Groton audience specifically. “This is not a work of theater in isolation,” he said.
Is there something you’ve yet to learn about that you’re really looking forward to? Joon is eager to now examine other plays through similar layers of lenses.
